title: Improving vaccination coverage and timeliness through periodic intensification of routine immunization: evidence from Mission Indradhanush
venue: Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences
abstract: Only an estimated 62% of Indian children under the age of 2 years are fully immunized. We examined the association between India's Mission Indradhanush (MI)-a periodic intensification of the routine immunization program-which was implemented in phases across districts between March 2015 and July 2017, and routine vaccination coverage and timeliness among children. We used data from a 2015 to 2016 national survey of children (n = 29,532) and employed difference-in-difference regressions to examine binary indicators of receipt of 11 vaccines and whether vaccines were received at recommended ages. The full immunization rate was 27% higher among children under 2 years old residing in MI phase 1 and 2 districts (intervention group) as compared with those residing elsewhere (control group). The rate of receiving all vaccines at recommended ages was 8% higher in the intervention group. Receiving doses of oral polio vaccine (OPV) birth dose, OPV dose 1 (OPV1), OPV2, OPV3, bacillus Calmette-Guérin, and hepatitis B birth dose vaccines were 9%, 9%, 11%, 16%, 5%, and 19% higher in the intervention group than the control group, respectively. More research is required on the cost-effectiveness of investing in MI-type programs as compared with routine immunization.

summary.oneLiner: Districts in India's Mission Indradhanush phases 1 and 2 were associated with higher full immunization rates and more on-time vaccination than other districts.
summary.overview: India's Mission Indradhanush is a periodic drive that intensifies the routine childhood immunization programme. The authors compare children under 2 in districts that received the drive in its first two phases (March 2015 to July 2017) with children in other districts, using a difference-in-differences design, which contrasts how coverage changed over time in the two groups. They find that full immunization was 27% higher in the intervention districts, and that receiving all vaccines at the recommended ages was 8% higher. The authors call for cost-effectiveness research comparing such drives with routine immunization before further investment.
summary.question: Is Mission Indradhanush, a periodic intensification of routine immunization rolled out in phases across Indian districts, associated with higher vaccination coverage and better timeliness among children?
summary.method: Difference-in-difference regressions, a method that compares the change over time in intervention districts (MI phases 1 and 2) with the change in control districts. The outcomes were binary indicators of whether a child received each of 11 vaccines and whether vaccines were received at recommended ages.
summary.data: A national survey of children conducted in 2015 to 2016 (n = 29,532), covering children under 2 years old. The programme was implemented in phases across districts between March 2015 and July 2017.
findings: Full immunization rate was 27% higher among children under 2 in MI phase 1 and 2 districts than in other districts.
The rate of receiving all vaccines at recommended ages was 8% higher in the intervention group.
Receipt of the OPV birth dose, OPV1, OPV2, OPV3, BCG and hepatitis B birth dose was 9%, 9%, 11%, 16%, 5% and 19% higher in the intervention group, respectively.
The authors note that an estimated 62% of Indian children under 2 are fully immunized, as background.
The authors state that more research is required on the cost-effectiveness of investing in MI-type programs as compared with routine immunization.
summary.whyItMatters: The paper suggests that periodic intensification drives can improve both coverage and timeliness of childhood vaccination, which is relevant to health policymakers allocating programme budgets. The authors indicate that cost-effectiveness evidence is still needed before judging whether such drives are a better use of resources than routine immunization.
